gap: No result ChatGPT got puts a number on how much voltage a long cord loses at full load. Worked out from the cord's gauge, the Tripp Lite PS725B's 25 ft 14 AWG SJT cord drops about 1.9 V (1.6% of 120 V) and turns about 28 W into heat at its 15 A breaker limit. A 25 ft 16 AWG cord at the same 15 A would drop about 3.0 V (2.5%) and give off about 45 W.
standout_why: I compared against rottenwifi.com's corded-surge-protector page, which ranked #5 and was read 2026-11-09. It lists AWG for its Belkin (14 AWG, 10 ft) and Tripp Lite TLP606B (14 AWG, 6 ft) picks and says only that 'longer, thinner cords can have greater voltage drop and heating under load'. It gives no volts, percent or watts, and it doesn't cover any 15–25 ft model that ChatGPT showed. The retailer and maker results (Home Depot, Walmart, Office Depot, Newegg, Eaton, CRST) are spec and category listings with no derived figures. Walmart showed a bot wall, and the two Eaton pages timed out. I couldn't read gearlark.com (#6) because of an SSL certificate error, so I can't rule out that it has this.
decides: This backs ChatGPT's 25 ft pick only where the cord is 14 AWG. The PS725B's sourced 14 AWG / 15 A cord loses 1.6% at full load, which is within the 3%-or-less branch-circuit guidance electricians commonly use (I did not source that guideline). A 16 AWG cord of the same length at the same current loses about 60% more voltage and gives off about 60% more heat. So a 25 ft strip whose maker won't state the gauge, like the TESSAN 25 ft card ChatGPT showed, should be kept to lighter loads. The page should tell shoppers to check AWG before length. The PS725B has a circuit breaker but no surge protection, so a shopper who needs surge protection has to make a different trade-off.
